newsitem.title: USA: Ill. gov presses GOP caucus on school funding plan.
newsitem.headline: Ill. gov presses GOP caucus on school funding plan.

text.p: Illinois Republican Gov. Jim Edgar conferred briefly with party legislative leaders Tuesday on education funding reforms and later met privately with other caucus members to bolster support for his plan, a spokesman said.

Spokesmen for the governor and other legislative leaders reported no progress on an education funding package Tuesday and lawmakers were growing less optimistic that they would meet their self-imposed Friday deadline for wrapping up the session.
Edgar has proposed a 25 percent personal income tax increase to generate $1.5 billion in revenues for property tax cuts and increased funding for school districts located in less affluent areas.
The governor's plan would provide up to $1.2 billion of property tax relief and $600 million for schools to bring every school district to a minimum of $4,225 per pupil.
The Edgar plan would raise the income tax rate from 3 percent to 3.75 percent, but when combined with property tax cuts, most homeowners would see a net tax reduction at least temporarily.

Republican legislators have raised the greatest opposition to their governor's proposed income tax hike, opposing it outright or offering a myriad of increases in other taxes to provide new money for education.

Senate President James "Pate" Philip and House Minority Leader Lee Daniels have voiced opposition to a 25 percent income tax hike, but have offered lesser income tax increases combined with other taxes.
Edgar met briefly with Philip and Daniels late Tuesday morning before holding one-on-one meetings with other members of the Republican caucus in the afternoon, spokesman Tom Hardy said.
The governor wanted to "talk with them get to know their concerns" about the school funding plan as he has with other issues, Hardy said.
"He calls in the legislators and tells them where he would like them to be," Hardy said of the meetings. "He tries to persuade them."

Edgar told Philip and Daniels on Tuesday that he stands by his proposal, but would approve a 3.6 percent income tax rate increase with an understanding that it would result in a smaller property tax relief package, Hardy said.
"The governor is not moving back and forth or up and down, he prefers the 3.75 plan, but he's not rigid about it, and would accept 3.6," Hardy said.

Daniels' spokesman, Brian Timpone, said that Daniels supports a 3.4 percent income tax increase combined with other taxes that would bring the poorer districts up to the base funding level within two years and phase in property tax relief over six years.
